text:
00-CV-188172CM

Zesta Engineering Ltd. V. Cloutier et al

Wall, J. for the moving party, plaintiff

Harris, D. for Cloutier, Kelvin and
Peatling

Diskin, M. for Christie

Fletcher, R.M. for Durante, Sanger and
White

REASONS

Master Haberman
:   This motion deals with how solicitor-client privilege is formed,
what can prevent its formation and how it can be lost in the context of a
complex legal proceeding involving a claim and counterclaim.  Both the claim
and counterclaim revolve around David Cloutier’s employment with and eventual
departure from the plaintiff, Zesta Engineering Inc.

Cloutier began working for Zesta in 1978
and by November 1999, he occupied the positions of vice president and assistant
general manager.  On November 27, 1999, his employment with Zesta was
terminated.    The action raises questions about Cloutier’s conduct before his
termination.

Zesta commenced this action, alleging that
they were justified in ending their relationship with Cloutier as he and some
of his colleagues had been plotting to leave and to set up a competitor
business.   In furtherance of that plan, Zesta says that Cloutier and the
others began taking Zesta`s goodwill as well as their confidential information
about suppliers and clients while still employed by Zesta.  Cloutier denies
this and counterclaims for wrongful dismissal.

Zesta has made a number of serious
allegations about how Cloutier conducted himself before his termination.  Among
them is their assertion that Cloutier diverted business from their supplier,
Watlow, to their customer, Husky, by steering a number of orders that should
have been processed by them to an entity known as Codlin Graphics Inc.
(Codlin).  They say Cloutier benefited directly from those orders while Zesta
lost the orders, and hence, income from these transactions.

As the action wended its way through the
court, its composition changed, such that parties were added and others
deleted.   In 2004, Douglas Christie, counsel to Cloutier, was added as a
defendant.

In September 2006, I was asked by Zesta to
deal with refusals arising from the examinations for discovery of several of
the defendants.    Among the issues before me at that time was whether
Christie, Cloutier`s former counsel, had properly claimed solicitor-client privilege
with respect to certain information and documents that were being sought from
him.  That privilege, to the extent it existed, belonged to Cloutier.

In the end, the parties agreed that
Christie would answer questions and produce documents, including any notes made
by Christie, regarding, among other things:

the
transactions involving Codlin Graphics Inc. in respect of which Cloutier has
waived solicitor-client privilege.
(see my order,
September 29, 2006)

The parties came before me again on October
10, 2006 by way of telephone case conference.  At that time, Christie was
ordered to:

Serve a
further and better affidavit of documents (dealing with the Codlin transaction)
by October 20, 2006.

In compliance with the order, Christie
swore a supplementary affidavit of documents on October 18, 2006, which he
served shortly thereafter.  In schedule “A” of that document, Christie
discloses four sets of handwritten notes that he prepared on four different
dates.  Each set is described as “handwritten notes prepared by Douglas
Christie with redactions,” and each, I am told, are Christie’s notes taken at
meetings with Cloutier.

The motion before me is to require Christie
to produce those notes in their entirety.   While Christie and some of the
defendants took no position on the motion, the relief sought was resisted by
Cloutier (he, Peatling and Kelvin are now all represented by the same counsel)
on the basis of solicitor-client privilege.   Cloutier’s position is that his
waiver of privilege was restricted to “the transactions involving Codlin.” As
the redacted portions of the notes make no mention of “the Codlin
transactions”, he says the notes remain subject to privilege, as there was no
general waiver that would extend to their contents.

The motion raises the following issues:

1)

Were Christie and Cloutier engaged in a process
involving the seeking or receipt of legal advice during any of the meetings
that generated these notes, such that solicitor-client privilege exists to
protect the notes from disclosure?

2)

Could privilege arise with respect to issues
discussed by Cloutier and Christie in the presence of others?

3)

If privilege did arise, has Cloutier waived it
by putting his state of mind in issue and relying on legal advice received and
acted upon to justify his actions?

4)

Can solicitor-client privilege be maintained in
the context of a party’s intention to commit a civil “unlawful act”?

5)

Do the notes contain facts or what could be
viewed as legal advice, and if both, should the notes be produced subject to
redaction of the privileged parts?

I have been made privy to the contents of
each of the four sets of notes in their entirety but will attempt to limit my
discussion of the notes to only those portions seen by Zesta counsel where
possible, so that in the event of an appeal of this decision, I will not have
overly disturbed the status quo.

A.
FACTUAL BACKGROUND

This motion arises in the context of
lengthy and complex piece of litigation that began more than eight years ago.
The original claim, which has now been amended twice, was not unlike many that
come before the court.  It involved allegations by a corporate entity to the
effect that its former employees left to set up a business that would
effectively compete with them, and that they took with them confidential
information to assist in their endeavours.

From his original statement of defence and
in his current pleading, Cloutier has asserted a counterclaim for wrongful
dismissal.   He has also endeavoured to justify a series of questionable
transactions, which Zesta calls the Codlin transactions, by suggesting that
his involvement in these events was limited to his having been engaged in a
sting operation to catch Jones, another Zesta employee who was allegedly
defrauding Zesta.

Douglas Christie was counsel to Cloutier at
the outset of the litigation.   The defendant Michael Jeffries retained
separate counsel from the commencement of the action.    These two, along with
an entity called Hi-Cap, were the original defendants named by Zesta.

The action moved through the court swiftly,
and was tried over the course of 20 days in January and February 2002.  The
decision of the trial judge was, in large part, overturned by the Court of
Appeal in the fall of that year, and a portion of the action was sent back to
be retried.

In February 2004, the statement of claim
was amended to add Christie and others as defendants to Zesta’s action.
Christie was joined on the basis of Zesta’s assertion that he was aware of some
of the things that Cloutier et al. had done and were doing, and that he
condoned these allegedly unlawful acts.  Zesta states that Christie was
complicit, wilfully blind or reckless.   It is also alleged that Christie
accepted payment of his fees for services rendered to Cloutier from Codlin
through a numbered company, although he was aware that these funds were
obtained as a result of Cloutier having diverted orders from Zesta.

Zesta devotes more than eight pages of its
pleading to the Codlin issues and Christie’s involvement with them, under the
heading “The Codlin Graphics Scheme to defraud Zesta”.    The allegations
involve the supply of band heaters.     On the basis of Zesta’s pleading, it
appears that the Buffalo branch
of Husky asked Zesta to source a quantity of a particular band heater that met
their specifications for Husky part number 534192.   Zesta asserts that
Cloutier turned to their supplier, Watlow, and placed 6 orders for a total of
319 band heaters in order to meet the request.   Zesta states that Cloutier had
Zesta staff stencil each heater with the Husky part number 534192 and that he
then moved the heaters off Zesta premises without sending them through Zesta’s
distribution department or entering them into inventory.

According to Zesta, Cloutier then advised
Husky Buffalo that he had the stock they needed but that they would have to
purchase the heaters from Codlin rather than Zesta.   Codlin is an Ontario corporation which Zesta says
carries on business as a print broker, not a manufacturer or distributor of
electric heaters for industrial application.   The president of Codlin, Brian
Burch, is allegedly Cloutier’s friend.

Zesta states that Cloutier repeated this
subterfuge and diverted further orders in this manner.  On the basis of these
assertions, Zesta claims that Cloutier earned in excess of $100,000 from the
sale of these heaters, after having improperly diverted Husky’s orders from
Zesta.

Zesta provided the court with excerpts from
the examinations for discovery of Christie (September 8, 2004; December 1,
2006) and of Cloutier (March 26, 2007) as well as the affidavits filed by
Cloutier and Jeffries in the context of Zesta’s motion for summary judgment to
show that either privilege was never formed or that if it did, it was waived.
There are inconsistencies in the evidence that must be discussed.

B.
ISSUES - Background

There are 4 sets of notes.  They are dated
October 21 (meeting 1), November 5 (meeting 2), November 9 (meeting 3) and
November 28, 1999 (meeting 4).  Cloutier’s employment with Zesta was terminated
on November 27, 1999 and this action was initiated on November 26 of that
year.   Both of these events fall between meetings 3 and 4.  Zesta alleges that
no privilege attaches to the notes of the meetings taken before November 26,
(meetings 1-3) as Cloutier and Christie were not yet in a solicitor-client
relationship and Cloutier denies that the meetings were anything more than
social.

Zesta also asserts that there were others
present when Cloutier met with Christie at meetings 2, 3 and 4.  On that basis,
they say no privilege could have arisen to protect those communications, as the
matters discussed were discussed openly and absent an intention to keep what
was said in confidence.

Zesta states further that Cloutier put his
state of mind in issue by claiming that his failure to divulge information
about the Codlin transactions was the result of his having acted on  legal
advice received from Christie.  Accordingly, they submit that any privilege
that may have attached to these communications with Christie has been waived.

Finally, Zesta submits that any
communications Cloutier had with Christie that he now seeks to protect by
privilege surround a common intention by him and Christie to perpetrate an
unlawful act, so they are therefore not covered by privilege.

Finally, it is asserted that at least some
of the information conveyed by Cloutier to Christie constituted “fact”.  The
question then arises as to whether documents should be produced in redacted
form so that the portions that are not privileged can be accessed.

As indicated earlier, the notes of all four
have been disclosed in schedule “A” of Christie’s supplementary affidavit of
documents and they have been produced in redacted form.

The portion of notes produced with respect
to meeting 1 simply say “Dave Cloutier” on the left and “Oct. 21 99” on the
right side of the page.

The produced portion of notes for meeting 2
has only the following notation:

Dave Cloutier
5 Nov 99

Derek
Peatling   at:
925 Meyerside Rd.

Mississauga

The meeting 3 notes produced are very
similar to those parts produced for meeting 2.  All that is different is the
date on the top right hand side (9 Nov 99) and there appears to be a time below
the address, “9-11:30”.

The portion of the notes of meeting 4 begin
“Cloutier ats Zesta” followed by the date “Nov 28/99.”  The following names
appear in a column on the left side beneath “Cloutier v. Zesta”: Joe Durante,
Mike Jeffries, Keith, Dave, Derek.  “Chris Chenowith/Harris + Assoc.” appears
opposite Jeffries.

Aside from the information set out above,
the various sheets of lined paper produced are completely blank.   The notes
for meetings 1 and 4 appear to have been contained on one page, only.  In the
case of meeting 2, there are 5 blank lined pages following the cover page, and
one blank lined page follows the cover page for meeting 3.

Some of the issues raised by Zesta as a
basis for saying they are entitled to see far more than these blank pages apply
to several, but not all of these notes.  I will take each issue in turn.

1
.
Were Cloutier and Christie
engaged in the process of seeking/providing legal advice at the time of
meetings 1, 2 and 3, such that Christie’s notes of those meetings are
privileged?

The Law

Solicitor-client privilege is often
described as one of the cornerstones of our system of justice.  There are
significant policy reasons to promote its existence and to ensure that it is
not lightly disturbed.  Our system of law encourages parties to feel free to
communicate in a frank and candid manner with counsel to facilitate their
having access   to the best possible legal advice.  If they are fearful that
their counsel may, at some future date, be compelled to disclose what they have
confided, it is bound to have a negative impact on what and how much they
confide in counsel.  As a result, a large body of law has emerged regarding the
importance of recognising and deferring to this privilege to protect from
disclosure solicitor-client communications.

At the same time, Ontario prides itself having established a civil legal process that is open
and fair to all parties.   The pre-trial steps in our Rules were designed to
ensure the utmost candour between parties, so that all issues are fleshed out
and all relevant information and documents are exchanged before trial.  This
approach promotes fair and early settlements and discourages what used to be
referred to as “trial by ambush”, something that has not been permitted in this
jurisdiction for some time.

How does one reconcile these competing
interests?  On the one hand, parties must be able to consult counsel in a
meaningful way to get the advice they need.  On the other, they must also be forthright
about their position and disclose information and documents that might not
assist their position and, in fact, might endanger it.  The general approach of
full and fair disclosure that applies in civil actions in Ontario is at odds with the concept of
privilege, which exempts otherwise relevant information and documents from
having to be produced.    The tension that exists between the two concepts has
resulted in careful consideration of what is required before this form of
privilege will be recognized, as well as a series of circumstances that could
lead to the privilege, once formed, being lost.

As a starting point, for communications
between an individual and a solicitor to be eligible for solicitor-client
privilege, those communications must have occurred in the context of that party
either seeking or the lawyer providing legal advice, or as Manes and Silver put
it “in the continuum” of communications between them (see Manes and Silver, ­
Solicitor-Client
Privilege in Canadian Law
, Butterworths: Toronto, 1993).  This extends to
information provided by the client to enable counsel to form her opinion and to
communications with a view to assisting counsel to decide whether or not to
take the case.    As Manes and Silver put it, even if advice is not expressly
requested, the expectation of receiving advice is implied when a
solicitor-client relationship exists and information is provided to enable the
lawyer to provide advice, either then or at a later date.

Thus, before this privilege can be successfully
invoked, the court must review the context in which the communications arose,
and be satisfied that the relationship of solicitor and client, in fact,
existed at the time of the communications or that the discussion took place
with a view to forming such a relationship, even if the meeting did not result
in a retainer.

The seminal case on point was decided by
the Supreme Court of Canada in 1982.   In
Descoteaux v. Mierawinski

1982 CanLII 22 (SCC)
, [1982] 1 S.C.R. 860, the court made the following comments which have a bearing
on this case:

When dealing with the right
to confidentiality it is necessary, in my view, to            distinguish
between the moment when the retainer is established and the moment     when the
solicitor-client relationship arises.  The latter arises as soon as the

potential client has his
first dealings with the lawyer’s office
in order to obtain      legal
advice.
(
emphasis added).

The items of information
that a lawyer requires from a person in order to decide   if he will agree to
advise or represent him are just as much communications made     in order to
obtain legal advice as any information communicated to him             subsequently.
It has long been recognized that even if a lawyer does not agree to             advise
the person seeking his services, communications made by the person to the             lawyer
or to his staff for that purpose are nonetheless privileged.

This does not mean that anything a person
tells his potential lawyer is covered by privilege.   The information conveyed
must be have been made “in the context of a solicitor-client relationship”,
that is, in the course of either providing information so as to obtain or the
actual provision of legal advice.  This privilege will not apply when advice is
“neither sought nor offered” (see
Toronto-Dominion Bank v. Leigh Instruments
Ltd.
1997 CanLII 12113 (ON CTGD)
, 32 O.R. (3d) 575;
Solosky v. The Queen

1979 CanLII 9 (SCC)
, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 821).
It will also not apply when the solicitor deviates from his role as solicitor
(see Manes and Silver (supra)).

Evidence

It is clear from all accounts that Christie
was retained after Cloutier’s employment with Zesta was terminated and that the
purpose of meeting 4 was to discuss the termination, and what to do about it.  Accordingly,
my comments under this section have no application to the notes created at
meeting 4, as Cloutier and Christie were, by November 28, 1999, in a
solicitor-client relationship.    This is conceded by all parties.

This rationale does not apply, however,
with respect to the notes of meetings 1-3, so the evidence must be reviewed to
assess the nature of the relationship between these two men at the time of each
of these meetings and what each thought they were talking about.

The most appropriate starting point is
Cloutier, himself, as he has invoked privilege.   On August 4, 2006, Cloutier
swore an affidavit in response to Zesta’s motion for summary judgment.  At
paragraph 72 of his affidavit, he states:

Soon after my termination, I retained Doug Christie
to deal with the Zesta civil action.  I gave Doug Christie full
details of the funds received from Codlin and details of these transactions as
noted above
(emphasis added)
.

As Cloutier was not terminated until
November 27, 1999, it appears that three earlier meetings took place before he
had actually retained Christie, at least, for the purpose of assisting him with
the action.  He makes no mention of having retained him earlier, for any other
purpose.  In fact, a review of Cloutier’s evidence makes it clear that, in his
view, there was no solicitor-client relationship between the two men until
after Cloutier’s employment was terminated, and he sought no legal advice until
after that event.

Cloutier was examined for discovery in
March 2007 and at that time, was asked when he first retained Christie.
Cloutier answers this in question 1968 and onwards, by explaining that he first
met Christie on a golf course.   After a series of questions it becomes clear
that this was strictly a social and unplanned encounter.

Cloutier was also firm about his having met
with Christie thereafter on a social rather than a business-basis.  He was
unequivocal when he stated that the meetings were not for the purpose of
obtaining legal advice.    At question 1980, he states:

Q:        When was the first
business or legally-related meeting that you had with     Mr. Christie?

A:        The day that I was
fired.

In terms of why Christie came to meetings
at the Multivest office, Cloutier responded, at question 1983:

A:        I remember him
coming to the Multivest office because he wanted to see    the operation.  He
didn’t come for any business meeting.

Finally, the following exchange took place
from questions 1987-1988:

Q:        But any meetings
you would have had with Mr. Christie prior to the date    of termination would
not have been of a legal advice nature?

A:        No.  Doug had an interest
in anything that was going on and I think when  he realized it was a real
estate company and things like that, you know,
he was        questioning and
I think trying to solicit opportunities but we didn’t need     anything legal
with that.

Q:
So I take it your
evidence is the first time you sought legal advice from   Mr. Christie was the
night you were terminated?

A:        Absolutely
.
(emphasis added)

Cloutier’s evidence is not qualified in any
way.  He does not suggest that the first time he sought legal advice from
Christie about his termination was after it had occurred – he maintained that
this was the first time he ever sought legal advice from Christie and that he
didn’t “need anything legal” before that.   Cloutier also states that Christie
was there for his own purposes – to see the operations and solicit
opportunities – rather than qua-solicitor, thus, not in the role of solicitor.

Christie’s evidence with respect to the
issue is somewhat but not entirely different.  Of concern is that his evidence
is not entirely consistent within itself regarding this issue.    Christie was
cross-examined on December 1, 2006 and essentially said that Cloutier solicited
legal advice from him at their first meeting after the golf course encounter.
However, when specifically asked about meeting 1, Christie replied that it was
in the nature of a “beauty contest”.    As Christie put it (questions 293 - 5)

A:        And basically, he
gave me a short description of what he was about and     his family situation
and wondered if I would agree to a more formal meeting to        discuss his
situation and whether he and I would be a good fit.  That is why I            call
it a beauty             contest.  I am sure you have been to them.

Q:        Again, referring
to the topic, did he go any further in describing the topic   of the legal
advice or representation he was seeking consistent with your   description of
the two later meetings?

A:        He just explained
his existing circumstances to me, that he had dedicated   a substantial part of
his life to a business in which he was not an owner.

Q:        And you understood
that
if he retained you, he would be seeking advice
from you in
relation to that?

A:        Exactly.
(Emphasis added)

Christie also testified that, between
meeting 3 and 4, he received a voice-mail message from Cloutier making it clear
that his services were not needed at that time.  As Christie put it (question
311), what Cloutier said was basically in the nature of “we are doing some
things on our own and we don’t really need to talk to you.  When we feel we should,
we will brief you.”

Earlier is his discovery, however, Christie
stated that the two meetings that took place at Peatling’s office did involve
the imparting of legal advice.  He stated, in response to question 274:

I think I can comfortably
say, but not go any farther than this, that
I was being     consulted on the
lawful discharge of the obligations of Cloutier as a fiduciary of   Zesta and
how he could make the transition out of Zesta
, but I can’t be more      specific
than that.
(emphasis added)

Christie also swore an affidavit in support
of this motion.  At paragraphs 9, 10 and 11 of his affidavit of December 13,
2007, Christie states that he provided Cloutier with legal advice at the
meetings of October 21, 1999 (meeting 1), November 5 (meeting 2) and November 9
(meeting 3).     His comments regarding meeting 1 are difficult to reconcile
with his description of that encounter along the lines of a “beauty show”.

Analysis and conclusion

How can this inconsistency in the evidence
be resolved?  On the one hand, we have Cloutier denying that anything he did or
said to Christie before his termination was in the nature of seeking or
receiving legal advice.   He goes further and says Christie came to speak with
him to stake out his own opportunities.   This is essentially what he says when
he was examined for discovery and it is consistent with his affidavit
evidence.    Christie, on the other hand, has provided evidence that is
somewhat equivocal regarding meeting 1, but suggests that he was giving legal
advice at the next two meetings.

As Cloutier is in the position of “client”,
it is his intention that should govern.  If he was simply chatting with
Christie but had no intention of retaining him during the course of these
meetings, it can’t be said that these communications were part of a continuum, with
Cloutier imparting information for the purpose of obtaining legal advice down
the road.   This should end the matter, with Christie’s understanding of events
being cast more as “wishful thinking” than an accurate rendition of what took
place.  How can he speak to what was in Cloutier’s mind?

But matters do not end there.  Despite
Cloutier’s clear and unequivocal evidence, his counsel now says I must ignore
what Cloutier has said and focus instead on the content of the notes, as they
will lead me to a very different conclusion, one that is contrary to what Cloutier
indicates in his evidence.   Counsel maintains that the notes themselves are of
such a nature that it is clear that Cloutier was providing information with a
view to getting legal advice.

There are several problems with this
approach.  To begin with, if I find that the contents of the notes of meetings
1-3 suggest that Cloutier must have been seeking legal advice so as to exempt
them from disclosure, I would be making a finding that is entirely inconsistent
with Cloutier’s own clear evidence.   This issue was carefully and thoroughly
canvassed with him at discoveries and he was steadfast in his position, to the
point of providing an explanation as to why Christie was present at these
pre-litigation meetings.

Counsel submitted that his client “may have
been wrong” about the meetings.  Although there may be room for a party to say,
in certain cases, that they misunderstood a question or the impact of a
response, there is no evidence to that effect.

If a party learns that information they
have conveyed during the course of their examination for discovery was not or
is no longer accurate, they are bound to correct it (see Rule 31-09(a) (b)).
No corrections have been made in this case.

I am also unable to say that Cloutier’s
evidence is completely inconsistent with what Christie has to say on the
subject, at least, in part, as Christie’s evidence is difficult to pin down.
Although Christie first says he believes he was given information with a view
to later providing legal advice, he also describes the first meeting as a
“beauty contest”, which, in the industry, generally means he was simply
“auditioning” for the brief but had not yet been retained.    This is also
consistent with Christie’s evidence about the voice-mail message he had
received between the 3
rd
and 4
th
meetings, telling him
his assistance was not needed at that time.

It is my view that Cloutier’s understanding
as to why the two were meeting ought to trump Christie’s.  Unless a party
intends to retain a lawyer as counsel, the lawyer’s hopes and wishes in that
regard are not really relevant.

On Cloutier’s own evidence, meetings 1, 2
and 3 did not involve the solicitation or the receipt of legal advice.   My
review of the notes of meeting 1 confirms Cloutier’s evidence.  While the notes
of meetings 2 and 3 could be interpreted to suggest otherwise, it would not, in
my view, be appropriate to enter into an interpretation exercise in the face of
Cloutier’s own very clear evidence, which stands uncorrected and unexplained.
Cloutier should not be permitted to make submissions on this motion that are
entirely inconsistent with his sworn evidence.

As a result, on the basis of Cloutier’s own
evidence as to his understanding, I am unable to say that he provided
information to Christie for the purpose of obtaining legal advice or that he
viewed anything that Christie may have told him as legal advice.    Unlike what
was before the court in
Descoteaux
, the information conveyed by Cloutier
was not to assist Christie in deciding whether or not he should accept the
retainer.  Rather, as Christie put it, this was a “beauty contest”, such that,
even on Christie’s evidence,  Cloutier was interviewing Christie as potential
counsel.

While Cloutier may have now had a change of
heart and wants to recharacterize what took place at those earlier meetings as
having involved the solicitation of legal advice, that is not his evidence
before me.  His counsel has adopted a rather cryptic approach, choosing to take
me back to the notes without attempting to explain the sudden shift aside from
suggesting that Cloutier may have been mistaken.

Accordingly, I find that the notes of
meetings 1, 2 and 3 are both relevant to the matters in issue between the
parties and not protected by privilege, as they were made during the course of
meetings that Cloutier did not intend or understand to be business or
legally-related encounters.     As far as he was concerned, the purpose of the
meetings was to advance Christie’s interests in seeking out opportunities, not
to provide Christie with information to be used down the road when he provided
legal advice.

Although this finding is sufficient to dispose
of the notes of meetings 1-3, I will deal with

those meetings, again in
the context of the other issues raised by this motion.

2
.
Did the presence of third
parties at meetings 2, 3 and 4  impede the formation of solicitor-client
privilege?

The Law

As noted earlier, the court must examine
the context within which communications were made to assess whether or not they
merit exemption from production on the basis of solicitor-client privilege.

One of the criteria needed to attract
privilege is that the communication in issue was intended to be confidential.
Two of the four requisite factors to attract this form of privilege referred to
in
Wigmore on Evidence
and discussed by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Slavutych
v. Baker et al.
1975 CanLII 5 (SCC)
, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 254 make the point:

1)

The communication must originate in a
confidence
that they will not be disclosed;

2)

This element of
confidentiality must be essential
to the full and satisfactory
maintenance of the relation between the parties.

As Manes and Silver state (supra):

Usually, the presence of a
third person hearing when the communication is made  indicates that the
communication was not intended to be confidential, unless such      presence is
reasonably necessary to protect  the client’s interests.    The better             rule
is that overheard solicitor-client communications remain privileged if:

(i)

the parties intended that their
communications be kept confidential; and

(ii)

the parties took reasonable steps to
ensure that the communication be kept confidential.

This requisite condition of privilege was
reiterated in
Toronto-Dominion Bank v. Leigh Investments Inc.
(supra),
where the court stated privilege will protect the communication “if it is
intended to remain confidential.”

The confidential nature of the communication
is therefore a hallmark of solicitor-client privilege and in its absence, no
such privilege can arise.   Both parties appear to accept this general
proposition.  Neither, however, provided any case law to establish, what, as a
matter of fact, will or will not qualify as an impediment to
confidentiality.    Does the intention to maintain confidentiality have to be
universal or can a communication be divulged to some people, while it is
expected to remain confidential from all others and still retain its privileged
nature?  Will the presence of a co-defendant while a matter is being discussed
necessarily denote that confidentiality was not intended?   Does it matter if
the party overhearing the communication has an identity of interest?  Does it
matter if they are represented by a different counsel?

The law appears to be clear that where
parties have a joint interest, such that they consult counsel together, what is
discussed during that joint session may still attract solicitor-client
privilege.   Similarly, where a solicitor and client communicate through a
third party or where they have sought the assistance of an expert, privilege
will arise if the parties intend the go-between or the expert to maintain
confidentiality with respect to their communications.  Beyond these scenarios,
each case will turn on its own facts.

Generally, the cases suggest that the party
who invokes privilege where he has communicated with counsel in the presence of
others must demonstrate on evidence that it was reasonably necessary for the
others to be present to advance his interest and that it was understood they
would maintain the confidence (see Sopinka,
The Law of Evidence in Canada

(Toronto and Vancouver: Butterworth’s, 1998).     While neither party provided
any case law on this point, it seems to me that these requisite criteria can
often be inferred from the identity of the third party and the
circumstances.    By way of example, a party may wish to have a family member
or close friend attend on counsel with him, to assist him in understanding what
counsel says and to help him remain calm.  Someone with a language barrier or
disability may also require a third party to assist in communicating with
counsel.  These scenarios present little difficulty and require little in the
way of explanation.

That, however, will not always be the case.

Evidence

It appears from the portion of the notes
that were produced that Cloutier and Christie were alone for meeting 1, so the
following discussion has no application with respect to the notes of that
meeting.

Derek Peatling was with the two of them for
meetings 2 and 3.   He has never personally been a client of Christie’s and was
only added to the action later in the day, along with Christie.    Peatling,
Jeffries, Durant and Sanger all attended meeting 4.   The evidence is not
consistent as to whether Jeffries’ counsel, Chris Chenoweth, was there, as
well.  The Notice of Action that was issued in November 1999 named only
Cloutier, Jeffries and an entity known as Hi-Cap Technologies as defendants,
such that Durant, Sanger and Peatling were not yet parties at the time of
meeting 4.   For some reason, a statement of claim was then issued in April
2000.  It included Durant, White, Sanger and Kelvin as defendants along with
Cloutier, and all of them came to be represented by Christie, but that was some
time after meeting 4.  This new claim did not include Jeffries or Hi-Cap.  None
of the defendants have crossclaimed against one another and Cloutier and
Peatling are currently represented by the same counsel.

This is what the parties had to say about
the meetings:

Michael Jeffries:  In his affidavit of
August 31, 2006, Jeffries explains that, though he was initially named as a
defendant, the action was resolved as against him in May 2000, so shortly after
the statement of claim was issued in the second action.   He states that he
attended meeting 4, which was convened at a small restaurant in Bolton.  He
says, at paragraphs 56-7:

While the whole group of us
was sitting around the table, multiple conversations   were taking place
simultaneously.  This meeting took place on November 28,  1999.  At this time
Zesta had commenced litigation against myself and Dave         Cloutier.

I heard Dave Cloutier ask
Doug Christie what they should do with respect to “the             heaters” and
how best to handle the situation.  Doug Christie advised Dave    Cloutier that
he had done nothing wrong and that the best thing he could do was      to do
nothing.  Outside the restaurant I asked Dave Cloutier what heaters he was             talking
about and he replied that it had to do with the axial clamp heaters shipped            to
Husky/Buffalo.  Dave Cloutier told me that Doug Christie had instructed him          that
it was best not to discuss the situation with anyone and as a result he       therefore
felt it best that we didn’t talk about it.  I respected his wishes and never             raised
the subject with Dave Cloutier again.

Doug Christie: During his examination for
discovery, Christie confirms that two of the meeting took place at Peatling’s
office and that Peatling was present at those meetings, at least, for the
beginning and the end (question 300).   Earlier in his evidence, Christie had
stated that Peatling was not a client “during the earliest period” but that he
had served the function of “host” for the meetings.   Christie assumed that
Peatling also served as Cloutier’s “advisor and friend.”   This is merely
Christie’s assumption, unsupported by evidence from Cloutier or Peatling to
that effect.

Christie goes on to say that “subsequently”,
Peatling was “part of a group behind Kelvin and Kelvin became a client.”
Further questions disclosed that Kelvin did not exist at the time of these
meetings, and only came to be in the early part of 2000.

Insofar as meeting 4, Christie confirms the
presence of the various defendants, but denies that Mr. Chenoweth was present.
He indicates that the reference to Chenoweth is simply to note that Jeffries
had retained him.

In his more recent affidavit, Christie
simply states that Peatling was “present for part of” meeting 2 and 3, without
being specific as to which parts.   He then lists those present for meeting 4,
this time saying that Chenoweth was present.  This evidence conflicts with what
Christie stated when he was examined for discovery earlier on.

This brings us to Cloutier.   It was
Cloutier’s evidence that all meetings that proceeded the day he was fired
(meeting 4) were social, rather than business meetings.   He states than
Cloutier attended at the Multivest offices “to see the operation” (question
1983) and “to try to solicit business opportunities” (question 1987).

There is no evidence at all from Cloutier
explaining why Peatling was involved in meetings 2 and 3, suggesting that he
was not present for any of the real discussions during that meeting or
indicating that Peatling was asked to keep what he had heard in confidence.
The fact that Peatling’s name appears on the top of Christie’s notes for both
of these meetings suggests that he did more than usher Christie into and out of
the facility.

There is no evidence from Cloutier or from
Peatling clarifying Peatling’s role or indicating that it had been made clear
to him that he was expected to retain in confidence what was discussed at these
meetings.   I was also not taken to any evidence to suggest that Peatling was
“family” or a close friend or business associate of Cloutier’s at the time of
any of these meetings, to explain his presence at these meetings.  Counsel
submits that I can infer why Peatling was present from the notes, themselves.
The notes are simply what Christie was told or heard or assumed, and wrote
down.  They are not in evidence to establish the truth of their contents.

Analysis and conclusion

As noted above, Cloutier’s counsel urges me
to rely on the content of the notes of these meetings as a basis for finding
that the meetings necessarily involved the solicitation and receipt of legal
advice.   In my view, it is not appropriate for me to have reference to the
notes in order to contradict Cloutier’s clear and express evidence.

It may well be that Cloutier gave his
evidence in the manner that he did at an earlier date as it served his purpose
to avoid any suggestion that he was seeking legal advice before his employment
with Zesta was terminated.  By indicating that none of these earlier meetings
involved legal advice, Cloutier may have been attempting to avoid speculation
as to why he was meeting with a lawyer at that time.   If he had not yet been
dismissed, what could they have been talking about?

But Cloutier has not come forward to say
that this is the case.  He has made no effort to correct, explain or put this
evidence in context, so it stands as is for the purpose of this motion.   It
would not be appropriate for me to simply ignore what Cloutier, himself, has
said, in order to accept his counsel’s submissions, when the two are
incompatible.   In the face of conflict between the evidence and the
submissions of counsel, the evidence must prevail.  Where the evidence is clear
and consistent, interpretive aids should not be relied on.   Finally, Cloutier
should not be permitted to rely on that evidence when it suits his purposes
while asking the court to ignore it when it doesn’t.  His failure to correct
the record to reflect what his counsel now suggests is the case is a critical
issue in my deliberations.

Cloutier’s evidence colours what took place
at meetings 1-3, and, in particular for the purpose of this discussion,
meetings 2 and 3.  If Cloutier says the meetings were of a social nature, only,
on what basis can the court infer that he intended the discussions to be kept
confidential in the absence of direct evidence to that effect?

In the event that I am not correct
regarding the first issue (whether these meetings involved seeking or obtaining
legal advice), my view is that Peatling’s presence at these middle meetings was
problematic.   The evidence is unclear – did he simply usher Christie in and
show him out, or was he present for any of the discussions at the beginning and
end of the meetings?   There is no evidence from either Cloutier or Peatling to
clarify that, but the fact that Peatling’s name appears at the top of the first
page of notes for each of these meetings suggests he did more than lead
Christie into and out of the room.

There is also no evidence from Cloutier to
explain why Peatling’s presence would have been necessary to advance his
interests, if he was, indeed privy to any part of the discussions, and to
indicate that it was made clear to him that he was required to keep what he
overheard in confidence.   The absence of any evidence on these points is
seriously problematic.   There is also no other evidence from which I can infer
that there was a good reason for Peatling to be present at these meetings.

Thus, on the basis of the limited evidence
on this point, I find that solicitor-client privilege never arose with respect
to the notes taken at meetings 2 and 3 in view of Peatling’s presence.

Meeting number 4 took place after
litigation was commenced and the evidence makes it clear that the topic of
discussion was the litigation, hence, the seeking and receipt of legal advice
was very much a part of this meeting.  There is, however, no explanation at all
as to why this group of men gathered to discuss these issues together with
Christie.  They were not defendants at that time, had no need to defend the
action and no basis for a counterclaim.  There is no evidence from any of them
that they were Christie’s clients in some other context, either.

There is also no context as to why
Jeffries, represented by separate counsel who may or may not have been present,
was included.  The fact that Jeffries retained his own counsel suggests some
concern of potential conflict.  How was his presence necessary to advance
Cloutier’s interests?   No evidence was filed to explain.  Further, although
Cloutier told Jeffries when he inquired, that he had been told by Christie not
to discuss the heaters, it appears Jeffries asked about it because Cloutier had
spoke openly and with sufficient volume about the heaters with Christie to have
been overheard at the meeting, such that Jeffries and possibly others did
overhear the discussion.  That, in my view, is not consistent with an intention
on Cloutier’s part to keep these discussions in complete confidence.  While he
may have formed the intention not to discuss these issues openly afterwards, as
a result of Christie’s advice, that was not his intention at the time of the
meeting, which, in my view, is the critical period.

In the context of the evidence before me,
the fact that the notes were taken during a meeting that involved a group of
people who were strangers to the action and whose presence at meeting 4 is
unexplained impedes the formation of solicitor-client privilege.   This flows
from the fact that one of the conditions precedent to the formation of
privilege, confidentiality, has not been met.   I therefore find that no
privilege attaches to the discussions that took place at meetings 2, 3 or 4, or
as a result, to the notes taken by Christie during those meetings.

3
.     Did Cloutier waive
solicitor-client privilege by relying on legal advice to account for his
conduct?

The Law

Solicitor-client privilege can be waived
expressly or by implication.  There is no suggestion here that Cloutier
expressly waived privilege, aside from what he views as a “limited” express
waiver contained in his counsel’s letter on his behalf regarding the Codlin
transactions.   Rather, Zesta maintains that Cloutier waived privilege by implication.
They submit that he put his state of mind in issue by attempting to justify his
actions on the basis of legal advice allegedly received and followed.

The applicable legal principle is well
stated in
Bank of Leu AG v. Gaming Lottery Corp.
[1999] O.J. No. 3949
.
There, Ground J. stated as follows:

When determining whether
privilege should be deemed to have been waived, the   court must balance the
interests of full disclosure for purposes of a fair trial            against
the preservation of solicitor-client and litigation privilege.  Fairness to             the
party facing a trial has become a guiding principle in Canadian law.     Privilege
will be deemed to have been waived where the interests of fairness and      consistency
so dictate or when a communication between a solicitor and client is        legitimately
brought into issue in an action.
Where a party places its state of        mind
in issue and has received legal advice to help form that state of mind,        privilege
will be deemed to be waived with respect to such legal advice.
(
emphasis
added)

The question then arises: if a party has
put their state of mind in issue by referring to legal advice, to what extent
has privilege been waived?   Does it apply only to that legal advice or to
surrounding facts?

The case law suggests that the waiver will
be deemed to be considerably broader than the specific advice.  In
Land v.
Kaufman

[1991] O.J. 1658
, Salhaney J. held that where privilege was deemed
waived, the party had to respond to “all questions pertaining to the communications”
she had with her counsel “on those subjects which are the subject matter of the
application.”  This would extend to what she told counsel, in addition to his
advice to her.

In expressing concern about a system that
might permit a party to reveal information that assists them while allowing
them to hide behind solicitor-client privilege, Salhaney J. quoted from Gale J.
in
Thomson v. Thomson et al.
[1948] O.W.N.137
, as follows:

It would be
an artful device to waive the privilege insofar as the precise wording of the
affidavit is concerned, but set it up to deprive the party of the right to
cross-examine on the affidavit.

Similarly, in
Leadbetter v. HMQ in right
of Ontario et al
.,
2004 CanLII 14107 (ON SC)
, 70 O.R. (3d) 224
,
Spence J. held that once an
otherwise privileged document is disclosed, any privilege that might apply to
other communications “as to the same subject matter” is deemed waived.  This,
he stated, avoids the risk of self-serving disclosure, such that a party
reveals those aspects that are helpful to his position while concealing those
that might hinder it.

Finally, in
Bentley v. Stone; Paterson
et al, Third Parties
,
1998 CanLII 14710 (ON CTGD)
, 42 O.R. (3d) 149, the court discussed the importance
of being able to test what a party asserts he told or was told by counsel by
way of cross-examination.    The opposing party should be able to check
accuracy by going beyond the strict wording of the affidavit.

Thus, as a matter of policy, it seems our
court has determined that a party cannot be selective in terms of the scope of
their waiver of privilege.   Once privilege has been waived with respect to a
particular subject matter, all communications about that subject matter can be
explored by the opposing party.

Evidence

Zesta relies on statements made by Cloutier
in his affidavit of August 6, 2006 as the basis for their position.  In
paragraphs 72-4, he states as follows:

Soon after my
termination, I retained Doug Christie to deal with the Zesta civil action.
I
gave Mr. Christie full details of the funds received from Codlin and the
details of these transactions as noted above.

I was advised by Mr.
Christie not to report the facts of these sales
because:

A.         The civil action
was “all about money”, and, thus, there would       ultimately be an accounting
and reconciliation of monies owed at the conclusion        of the civil action
and the counterclaim; and

B.         It had yet to be
determined who was to share in the distribution of said       proceeds, how
they were to be distributed, and to what extent each party would         benefit.

At this time I was extremely
distressed and emotionally upset.  In the summer of    2000 my depression was
at its zenith.
I followed the advice I had received from       Mr.
Christie.
I agree with the passing of time I should have disclosed the
funds         from the sale of these heaters immediately after my termination
to both Watlow    and Vince Eastman.
(emphasis
added)

Analysis and conclusions

Given the state of the law, it is difficult
to treat Cloutier’s evidence as anything other than a waiver of any privilege regarding
his discussions with Christie about the subject in issue.  He makes it clear
that, though he now appreciates what he ought to have done, he concealed
information at an earlier time as a result of what Christie told him, which
amounts to legal advice.

In terms of the scope of the waiver,
Cloutier’s evidence is the guiding factor.   Cloutier tells us that he provided
Christie with full details of funds received from Codlin, as well as full
details of the transactions – these are referred to as two separate things.  This
evidence was contained in a carefully drafted affidavit, rather than elicited
during cross-examinations.   Cloutier would have had an opportunity to review
his answer and consider it before swearing that it was true.  Affidavit
evidence is therefore different than a spontaneous response to one of a series
of a questions posed to a nervous witness at a table.  It must be the case that
each word and phrase is there because it was intended to be and that each must
have its own meaning.   Thus, the use of two phrases – “full details of the
funds received” as well as” full details of the transactions” must be taken to
refer to two separate things.

It is also important to bear in mind that
Christie, too, is now a defendant in this action, on the basis of allegations
as to his complicity.  It will therefore be important at trial for the court to
know what Cloutier was told by Christie before he gave the advice that Cloutier
maintains he received from him and acted upon.   How much did Christie actually
know about why and how monies were paid to Codlin before he advised Cloutier in
the manner that Cloutier suggests?

Thus, it is not simply the “details of the
funds received” that must be disclosed.   Cloutier’s waiver extends to the
“full details of the transactions”, which, in my view, goes beyond the dates,
amounts, prices and profits of each order.  It seems to me that “full details
of the transactions” means just that  and includes the background of each
transaction, the respective roles of Watlow and Husky in the context of the
transactions, as well as how and why Codlin became involved in the shipment of
parts between the two.  Counsel concedes that “Codlin” need not be referred to
expressly for privilege to have been waived, but he suggests the waiver is
restricted to the flow of money.  How can the flow be understood in the absence
of Watlow and Husky’s respective roles?

Cloutier also speaks in his affidavit as to
why Christie believed he should refrain from talking about the Codlin affair at
that stage.  By getting into the issue of how the proceeds were to be
distributed, any privilege that may have covered discussions between Cloutier
and Christie about this issue has also been waived.

As a result of the foregoing, on my review
of the notes, I find that any privilege that may have arisen with respect to
the notes taken by Christie at meetings 1, 2 and 3 is deemed to have been
waived by Cloutier’s reliance of legal advice to form his state of mind.

4
.
Are Cloutier and
Christie’s communications protected by privilege if information was conveyed by
Cloutier with the intention of committing an unlawful act – “future criminal
and fraud exception”?

The Law

Our law has long recognized an exception to
solicitor-client privilege in the context of the client alerting counsel to
plans to commit an unlawful act.  For the most part, this exception has been
invoked in cases where the acts contemplated were criminal in nature.

Dickson J. articulated the ambit of the
exception in
Solosky v. The Queen
,
[1980] 1 S.C.R. 835
as follows:

More significantly, if a
client seeks guidance from a lawyer in order to facilitate    the commission of
a crime or a fraud, the communication will not be privileged            and it
is immaterial whether the lawyer is an unwitting dupe or a knowing      participant.

As the application of this exception was
said to apply with reference to “a crime or fraud”, courts were able to say
that the Supreme Court intended this exception to operate beyond the ambit of
situations where the act discussed was strictly criminal.   Thus, in
Goldman,
Sachs & Co. v. Sessions

1999 CanLII 5317 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2815, Smith J. was prepared
to include the following torts within the ambit of the exception: abuse of
process, breaches of regulatory statutes, breaches of contract and other
breaches of duty.

Perell J. followed
Goldman
in
Dublin
et al. v. Montessori Jewish Day School of Toronto et al.
(2007)
2007 CanLII 8923 (ON SC)
, 85 O.R.
(3d) 511 and applied this exception to privilege in a wrongful dismissal case.
Here, the plaintiff was permitted to retain an e-mail that had been
inadvertently disclosed to him, as the court felt that its contents showed an
intention to commit various intentional torts, thus furthering the plaintiff’s
efforts to demonstrate that the defendants acted with malice and in bad
faith.

One aspect that is critical for this
exception to privilege to arise is that the communication in issue must concern
acts that are being contemplated, as distinct from those that have already been
committed.   In fact, the exception is often referred to as the “future crimes
and fraud” exception, in both case law and legal texts.   This exception is
justified on the basis that the communications involve future acts, as the
policy rationale for its existence is to curtail the possibility of lawyers
assisting clients by providing advice to facilitate the commission of offences,
either knowingly or not.    Thus, it is important, when reviewing particular
solicitor-client communications to assess the extent to which they deal with what
has already been done as opposed to what may take place.

The onus of proving that the exception
applies lies with he who claims it.  According to Smith K. in
Goldman

(supra), the court is not required to weigh conflicting evidence and make
findings of fact in order to determine that the exception applies.  On the
other hand,  there must be more than a mere allegation of a tort.  Some prima
facie evidence of the unlawful act must be tendered before the privilege will
be swept aside.   As Smith J. put it, the court should examine the moving
party’s position in the context of all evidence and surrounding circumstances
to determine if the communication in issue “gives colour to the charge.”

Evidence, analysis and conclusion

In this case, fraud has been alleged, so to
the extent that the communication speaks to an intent to commit that fraud,
this exception to privilege could apply, if all other requisite aspects of the
exception fall into place.    The other torts alleged against Cloutier are
breach of fiduciary duty and interference with economic relations, conversion,
breach of contract and conspiracy, not dissimilar from those that arose in
Goldman

(supra).

On the basis of the current state of the
law, I find that the exception to this privilege is available in the context of
these torts.

The next question is whether Zesta has met
their onus to be permitted to successfully invoke the exception: is there some
prima facie evidence of their assertions against Cloutier?    Cloutier,
himself, has now acknowledged that he was involved in the sale of these heaters
in a manner that was not disclosed to Zesta at the time of the sales or even
afterwards.  In his affidavit, he explains his failure to disclose this
information by referring to the legal advice he obtained from Christie and he
suggests that he followed the advice as he was in a vulnerable state.  Though
he says he now knows that was wrong, he has not amended his pleadings to drop
his defence regarding the alleged “Jones sting”.  That, in my view, is
sufficient to meet Zesta’s onus.

The final issue is whether these
communications deal with Cloutier’s past actions or future intentions.    There
is nothing about future intentions in the notes of meeting 1, which, for the
most part, deal with facts and Cloutier’s opinions.   The notes of meeting 2
suggest that was a very different type of meeting and that while further facts
were conveyed to provide background, there is a very definite sense that
Cloutier was also laying out his plans for the future and all that they
entailed.   Meeting 3 appears to have touched on those plans again, and meeting
4 did, as well, though less so.

On that basis, I find that to the extent
that solicitor-client privilege ever applied to the notes of the meetings, the
notes of meetings 2, 3 and 4 fall within the “future crime and fraud” exception
to solicitor–client privilege, such that any privilege that may have arisen
cannot protect the notes from being produced in their entirety.

5
.
Facts
are not privileged communications
:
redaction
of documents

As noted, Christie has disclosed the
existence of the meetings and the notes by producing the front page of each
set, with only the date and participants visible.  The remainder of each page
in each set of notes has been redacted out.   There was no evidence filed by
Christie to explain why he chose to do this and his counsel attended the motion
and took no position.   Essentially, it appears that, having alerted everyone
to the fact that the meetings occurred and that Christie took notes at the
meetings, he was prepared to leave the issue of privilege in the court’s
hands.

I find this to be at odds with what
Christie has said in his evidence about the meetings.  Despite Cloutier’s
adamant assertion that he was not looking for legal advice at any of the first
three meetings, Christie, at times, suggested that his understanding of things
was different – he felt that he had been called upon to provide advice of a
legal nature and that he did so.  Presumably, that is why he failed to disclose
the contents of any of the notes.  While the fact that meetings took place, the
dates of those meetings, the participants at each and his having taken notes
would not be protected as privileged communications, if he was of the view that
what was said at the meetings and what he noted down was privileged, the scope
of his disclosure was perfectly appropriate.

Despite that, however, it seems Christie
was not prepared to come forward on the motion to either explain that this was
his thinking or to support Cloutier’s attempts to protect any of the information.
Thus, it is possible, in view of Cloutier’s evidence, that Christie is no
longer prepared to stand behind his own evidence as to whether or not legal
advice was sought or conveyed at these meetings, and thought it best to leave
it to the court to sort out.

That brings us to the contents of the
notes.  The notes of meeting 1 are, in my view, simply factual, and include
some opinions.  There is nothing in the notes which I find to be in the nature
of a solicitor-client communication.  Thus in addition to all of the above
reasons, I find that no privilege attaches to these notes.

With respect to meeting 2, pages 1 and 2
are again a mix of fact and opinion.  Page 3 deals with future plans, while
both pages 4 and 5 are mixed but deal mostly with future events.   The notes of
meeting 3 speak mostly about the status quo, as do those of meeting 4, but in
each case, there is some reference to future plans.  As the privileged and
non-privileged information is intertwined in the notes of the three later
meetings, if I were to find that the notes of those meetings were privileged
and that the privilege had not been waived, it would be my view that no part of
the notes of those meetings should be or should have been produced.  In other
words, these documents should not have been disclosed in schedule “A” and
produced in redacted form.  While Christie was required to disclose the fact,
date and location of each meeting and a list of participants at each, he ought
to have disclosed the notes in schedule “B” of his supplementary affidavit of
documents if, in his view, their content was in any way privileged.

Summary of conclusions

Notes of meeting one:
shall be produced.  They deal with facts only, not privileged
communications so there was never any basis to protect them.  Cloutier has also
denied that the meeting that gave rise to the notes was intended by him as a
vehicle for seeking or obtaining legal advice.

Notes of meeting two:
shall be produced as, in this instance, too, legal advice was
neither sought nor provided, according to the “client”.  Further, the
unexplained presence of a third party detracts from any possible inference that
the communications were intended to be kept confidential.  Even if privilege
had arisen, it was waived by Cloutier as he relied on legal advice as the basis
for keeping these transactions from Zesta.   Finally, it appears that the
communications that took place at this meeting could well have involved the
commission of future unlawful acts, as defined by the cases, such that they
would fall under an exception to privilege.

Notes of meeting three:
shall be produced for all of the reasons listed with respect to the
minutes of meeting 3.

Notes of meeting four:
shall be produced.   In view of the crowd around the table and the
complete lack of evidence to explain why each was there, Cloutier is hard
pressed to establish that he intended his discussions with Christie on this
occasion to remain confidential.  Thus no privilege arose here.    If it did,
it was waived by Cloutier’s reliance on legal advice to justify his actions.
Finally, the notes go into some detail as to what Cloutier and some of the
others were planning, according to Cloutier.   On that basis, these
communications are not eligible for solicitor-client privilege, under the
“future crime and fraud” exception.

Accordingly, copies of all four sets of
notes shall be provided within 30 days.   I can be spoken to regarding costs at
the end of the motion, which is scheduled to resume on February 14, 2008.
